T1.text:
Hi everyone, for Table 1, we found Q3.5 and Q3.6 about sensitive data types a bit hard to answer because it was tricky to decide what counts as an acceptable improvement when using more personal information. The questions were clear but required making some tough trade-offs.

We thought the most important questions for how the model should be designed are:
  • Q3.4 on Absalon data—using this feels too invasive and risks flagging students unfairly
  • Q6.1 about personalized outreach—this needs to be balanced so it's helpful but not overwhelming

We noticed big differences in answers on these questions, probably because advisors want to help as many students as possible while students are more worried about privacy and avoiding unnecessary stress from too much contact.

One idea we had that didn’t fit the survey is creating a student-led review process where affected students help set guidelines for using sensitive data—this could make sure policies are fair and respectful.

Thank you S1! To add to that, I'd highlight our table's consensus on Q7.2—the balance between personalized outreach and not overwhelming students. We think a hybrid approach with automated but personal check-ins could work well.

We also believe the split in answers reflects different priorities: advisors focus more on effectiveness, while students prioritize privacy and avoiding unnecessary stress. Our idea for a student-led review process would help bridge this gap by ensuring policies are shaped by those most affected—students themselves.
[Word count: 72]

T2.text:
Thank you all for this discussion. At Table 2, we found that some questions about explainability levels were unclear and hard to answer because they were abstract without concrete examples.

The most important question for our table was Q4.1 on explainability levels. We believe high explainability is crucial because it builds trust between students and advisors. Understanding why support is offered helps students accept and use the help effectively.

We also found that opinions differed significantly on Q6.2 about outreach frequency. While many chose "continuously," we discussed how this could feel overwhelming and intrusive, especially if not personalized well. We prefer a balanced approach, like twice a semester check-ins with optional deeper support when needed.

Another idea that came up is the importance of ensuring that students can opt-out of contact if they feel uncomfortable with any form of outreach. This respects our boundaries while still providing necessary support.

Thank you for this valuable discussion.

I’d like to add that we also found Q6.1 on intervention types important because personalized emails must balance specificity with respect for privacy. Examples like “We noticed you missed some deadlines” help strike this balance.

Additionally, we discussed how creating clear examples of explainability levels and personalized emails will guide us in designing a model that respects student needs while providing effective support.

Thank you all for sharing your insights; it has been very valuable for our discussion.

T3.text:
Thank you for this great discussion! Our table found Q5.2 and Q6.1 really important because they focus on fairness and how we support students best. We struggled a bit with Q7.2—some of us wanted to reach more students with personalized messages, while others thought it should be more selective.

We had some different ideas about how selective the model should be for personalised messages (Q7.2). Some people wanted to reach out to as many students as possible because any help could make a difference. Others thought we should focus on students who clearly need extra support so that the messages feel thoughtful and not overwhelming.

We came up with an idea: start with a general email for everyone, then follow up with personalised messages if needed. This way, all students get support without feeling pressured or singled out. Thank you!

Thank you, S7. I agree that Q5.2 and Q6.1 are crucial for ensuring fairness and effective support.

We also discussed how to balance outreach efforts effectively. For personalized messages (Q7.2), some of us believed reaching more students could provide timely help, while others emphasized careful selectivity to avoid overwhelming or stigmatizing students.

Our table proposed a two-step approach: start with a general email for all students and follow up with personalized messages when needed. This ensures broad support while being thoughtful about individual needs.

Additionally, we highlighted the importance of clear explanations in personalized messages to make them feel supportive rather than invasive.

Thank you for this insightful discussion!
A3
